sights.address: 1400 John F Kennedy Blvd, Philadelphia, PA 19107
sights.w: The largest municipal building in the US, crowned by Alexander Milne Calder's 37-ft William Penn; a 100-year-old elevator lifts four at a time to the glass-enclosed deck 548 ft up, the city's only 360° view.

sights.address: 1599 John F Kennedy Blvd, Philadelphia, PA 19102
sights.w: John F. Kennedy Plaza, nicknamed for Robert Indiana's LOVE sculpture — one of Philly's most photographed spots, diagonal from City Hall. Free.
One of William Penn's five original squares, named for astronomer David Rittenhouse — the elegant heart of Center City for benches, people-watching and the Saturday farmers' market.
Penn's southeast square, a Revolutionary-era burial ground now holding the Tomb of the Unknown Revolutionary War Soldier; part of Independence NHP.
The 1873 Norman-cathedral-style headquarters of Pennsylvania's Freemasons across from City Hall, with seven lavish lodge halls in Egyptian, Moorish, Gothic and other styles; public tours.
Neoclassical waterworks pavilions (1815–) on the Schuylkill below the Art Museum — a National Historic Landmark with a free interpretive center and the classic river-and-boathouse view.

sights.n: Cathedral Basilica of Saints Peter and Paul
sights.w: Pennsylvania's largest Catholic church (1864) and the only US cathedral in the Roman-Corinthian style, modelled on Rome's San Carlo al Corso, on Logan Square.
Rafael Viñoly's glass-vaulted arts centre (2001); its cello-shaped, mahogany Marian Anderson Hall is home to the Philadelphia Orchestra, and the rooftop garden is free.
America's oldest grand opera house still used for its original purpose (1857): gilded, chandeliered home of Opera Philadelphia and the Pennsylvania Ballet.

sights.n: Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts (PAFA)
sights.w: The nation's first art museum and school (1805), in Frank Furness's Victorian Gothic landmark fronted by Claes Oldenburg's 51-ft Paint Torch — American art from Peale to the present.
Mother church of the first Black denomination in the US (founded 1787 by Richard Allen) on the oldest parcel continuously owned by African Americans; the basement museum holds Allen's tomb.
Free-standing 1786 Federal mansion of Dr. Philip Syng Physick, 'father of American surgery', who treated Dolley Madison and Andrew Jackson — with the instruments he invented.
One of the finest Georgian townhouses in America (1765), where Mayor Samuel Powel and Elizabeth Willing Powel entertained Washington, Adams and Franklin.
The largest Quaker meeting house in the world by seating (1803–04), whose abolitionist congregation expelled members who would not free enslaved people.
A Quaker family's 1768 house that became a key Underground Railroad station (Harriet Tubman is said to have stopped here) — a National Historic Landmark.
Quaker homestead begun 1690 — Revolution-era field hospital, later a brewery — whose 1820s rose garden is the nation's oldest in its original plan.
The 1744 Wister family house, British General Agnew's quarters in 1777, with North America's oldest female ginkgo in the garden.
America's second-oldest rural garden cemetery (1836): 74 sculpted acres of Victorian monuments high above the Schuylkill in East Falls — tours and moonlight events.
Where George Washington lived in 1793–94 to escape the yellow-fever epidemic — the oldest surviving presidential residence; NPS-run.

sights.address: 8231 Old York Rd, Elkins Park, PA 19027
sights.w: Frank Lloyd Wright's only synagogue (1954–59), a translucent glass-and-steel 'mountain of light' — one of four synagogues in the US that are National Historic Landmarks; tours by appointment.
650 acres of woods, meadows and old trees with 17 miles of trails — one of the region's oldest and largest public gardens, with giant treehouses for kids.
Pennsylvania's oldest church (1700), built by Swedish colonists in Queen Village — a National Historic Site with a riverside churchyard.

sights.address: 1 Lincoln Financial Field Way, Philadelphia, PA 19148
sights.w: Home of the Eagles in the South Philadelphia Sports Complex — tailgate culture at its loudest.
The Phillies' ballpark, where the concourse food is a Philly tour in itself (cheesesteaks, roast pork, Bull's BBQ) and the Liberty Bell lights up for home runs.
Olmsted Brothers-designed lakes-and-lawns park at the bottom of Broad Street, with the Swedish-American Museum next door and a skatepark under I-95.
The nation's first naval shipyard turned office-and-park campus with a central green and Delaware riverfront; the USS New Jersey was built here.
